questions.stem: A market is allocatively efficient when:
options: firms produce their current output at the lowest possible cost per unit
firms adopt new technology and products quickly over time
every household receives an equal share of total output
resources produce the mix of goods and services that society values most
questions.explanation: Allocative efficiency is about producing the right goods in the right quantities, where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost. Lowest-cost production is productive efficiency.

questions.stem: A supermarket chain installs self-service checkouts and automated warehouses, cutting its cost per item sold. This mainly improves:
options: equity in distribution
productive efficiency
allocative efficiency
dynamic efficiency
questions.explanation: Producing the same output with fewer resources lowers average cost, which is productive efficiency. Dynamic efficiency concerns adapting and innovating over time, although the investment may also reflect it.

questions.stem: Dynamic efficiency in a market is best shown by:
options: prices settling at the level where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
the government setting prices to guarantee fair returns to producers
firms innovating and adjusting their products and processes as conditions change
firms producing their current output at the lowest possible average cost
questions.explanation: Dynamic efficiency is the ability to respond over time to changing tastes, technology and costs. Producing current output at lowest cost is productive efficiency at a point in time.

questions.stem: A free market produces the quantity of a good where private benefit equals private cost, but the good's production harms nearby residents. Compared with the socially desirable outcome, the market outcome is:
options: optimal for society, because the residents can choose to move
optimal for buyers and sellers but too large for society as a whole
socially desirable, because the market reached equilibrium
too small, because producers do not count the harm done to nearby residents
questions.explanation: The private optimum ignores external costs, so output is higher than the level where social benefit equals social cost. A market can be in equilibrium yet still be socially undesirable.

questions.stem: Many Australian industries, such as banking, grocery retailing and airlines, are oligopolies. A key economic force behind this is:
options: very low start-up costs that let many small firms enter freely
government rules that require every industry to have many sellers
identical products that leave firms no way of competing
large economies of scale in a relatively small national market
questions.explanation: Where large scale cuts unit costs greatly, a small market can support only a few firms of efficient size, and high set-up costs deter entry. Low entry costs would encourage many sellers, not few.

questions.stem: A firm with substantial market power is most likely to cause a loss of allocative efficiency because it:
options: produces more output than consumers wish to buy
must accept the market price set by many competitors
is forced by its rivals to adopt new technology faster than they do
restricts output and raises price above the competitive level
questions.explanation: With few competitors, a dominant firm can earn higher profit by supplying less at a higher price, so fewer resources go to a good that consumers value. Price takers exist only in perfectly competitive markets.

questions.stem: Complete market failure (a missing market) occurs when:
options: the market does not supply a good or service at all
the market supplies too much of a good that harms others
the market supplies too little of a good with external benefits
the price of a good is set above its equilibrium level
questions.explanation: A missing market means no market forms, as with pure public goods such as national defence or street lighting. Over- or under-supply is partial market failure.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of partial market failure?
options: No private market develops to supply national defence
No firm can profit from building a lighthouse that guides all passing ships
A free market produces less education than is socially desirable
No firm offers to provide street lighting for a suburb
questions.explanation: The education market exists but under-provides because buyers ignore the external benefits, which is partial failure. Street lighting, defence and lighthouses are public goods that markets may not supply at all.

questions.stem: Why does the free rider problem lead markets to under-provide public goods?
options: Governments ban private firms from supplying public goods
People can benefit without paying, so firms cannot charge enough to cover costs
Public goods are too expensive for any household to want to consume
One person's use of a public good always leaves less of it for everyone else
questions.explanation: Public goods are non-excludable, so people have an incentive to let others pay, and private firms cannot collect enough revenue. Public goods are also non-rival, so one person's use does not reduce what is left for others.

questions.stem: The excesses of boom and bust in the economic cycle are a form of market failure because:
options: booms always raise living standards for every group in society equally
busts encourage firms to cut costs, which improves productive efficiency
governments cause every boom and bust through their spending
over-investment in booms and idle resources in busts misallocate resources
questions.explanation: In a boom, speculative investment and rising prices can pull resources into uses that later prove unprofitable; in a bust, workers and capital sit idle. Both outcomes are sub-optimal and socially undesirable.

questions.stem: On a diagram for a good whose production creates pollution, the marginal social cost (MSC) curve lies above the marginal private cost (MPC) curve. The vertical gap between them represents:
options: the tax the government already collects on each unit
the private benefit gained by consumers per unit
the external cost imposed on third parties per unit
the profit earned by the producer on each unit
questions.explanation: MSC = MPC + external cost, so the gap measures harm to others that the producer does not pay for. It is not a tax unless the government imposes one.

questions.stem: For a good with a negative externality in production, the free market produces at Qm, but the socially optimal output is Q*. The welfare loss triangle on the diagram lies:
options: between MSC and MPC, from Qm to the axis, covering all output
below the demand curve, from Qm to Q*, where output is too low for society
between MSC and demand, from Q* to Qm, where social cost exceeds benefit
between MPC and demand, from zero to Q*, where consumers gain
questions.explanation: Each unit between Q* and Qm costs society more than it is worth, so the triangle bounded by MSC, demand and the two quantities is the welfare loss. The market over-produces, so Qm lies beyond Q*.

questions.stem: Vaccination creates a positive externality in consumption. Compared with the socially optimal level, the free market will:
options: under-produce vaccines because the private cost exceeds the social cost
under-consume vaccines, with a welfare loss from benefits not gained
over-consume vaccines, with a welfare loss from excess production
consume the optimal quantity, as people value their own health
questions.explanation: Marginal social benefit exceeds marginal private benefit, so buyers stop short of the socially optimal quantity. The lost net benefit between the market and optimal quantities is the welfare loss.

questions.stem: Loud music from a backyard party disturbs neighbours late at night. This is an example of:
options: a negative externality of production
a positive externality of production
a negative externality of consumption
a positive externality of consumption
questions.explanation: The party-goers are consuming, and the cost falls on neighbours outside the decision, so it is a negative consumption externality. A factory's pollution would be a production externality.

questions.stem: Bees kept by a honey producer pollinate a neighbouring orchard, raising its fruit yield. This is an example of:
options: a positive externality of consumption
a public good provided by the government
a positive externality of production
a negative externality of production
questions.explanation: The honey producer's production benefits a third party who does not pay for it. As the benefit is not counted, the free market may produce less honey than is socially optimal.

questions.stem: Coal miners lose their jobs when a mine closes, but they lack the skills that growing industries need. This is an example of:
options: geographical immobility of labour
the free rider problem
a positive externality
occupational immobility of labour
questions.explanation: Occupational immobility means workers cannot easily move between jobs because their skills do not match new roles. Geographical immobility is about difficulty moving location.

questions.stem: Workers in a regional town where jobs are disappearing do not move to a city with job vacancies because housing there is much more expensive. This is an example of:
options: geographical immobility of labour
occupational immobility of labour
asymmetric information
the tragedy of the commons
questions.explanation: High housing costs, family ties and moving costs can stop workers relocating to where jobs are. Resources then stay idle in one place while shortages persist in another.

questions.stem: Why can the immobility of factors of production lead to a misallocation of resources?
options: Firms cannot produce any output at all without perfectly mobile factors
Resources cannot move quickly to uses where they are valued more highly
Immobile resources are always used where they are valued most
Prices stop sending signals about where resources are needed
questions.explanation: The price mechanism signals where resources are wanted, but if labour and capital cannot move, shortages and unemployment can exist side by side. The signals still work; the response to them is slow.

questions.stem: Extending property rights can help resolve the tragedy of the commons because:
options: owners have an incentive to conserve a resource they will benefit from later
it allows everyone to use the resource without any limit
it ensures the resource becomes a public good for all to share
it transfers the resource to whichever user can extract it the fastest
questions.explanation: When a resource is owned or access is controlled, the owner bears the cost of overuse and gains from conserving it. Open access gives each user an incentive to take as much as possible before others do.

questions.stem: An exclusive economic zone gives a country sovereign rights over the fish up to 200 nautical miles from its coast. In economic terms, this mainly:
options: turns the fish stocks into a pure public good available to all other nations
removes the need for any limits on how many fish are caught
creates a positive externality for foreign fishing fleets
extends property rights over a common resource so its use can be managed
questions.explanation: Defining who controls a resource allows a country to set quotas and licences, reducing the overuse common to open access. Exclusive economic zones are set under the international law of the sea.

questions.stem: Space junk in orbit threatens satellites operated by many countries and firms. Government options for addressing it are limited mainly because:
options: satellites create positive externalities that offset the damage
one country can easily force all others to clean up their debris
no one owns orbital space, so action needs costly global coordination
space junk is a private good that markets already price correctly
questions.explanation: With no common ownership and no single authority, each country has an incentive to free ride on others' clean-up efforts. Global warming raises the same coordination problem.

questions.stem: People who know they are likely to need expensive medical care are the most eager to buy health insurance. This is an example of:
options: the free rider problem
adverse selection
moral hazard
a positive externality
questions.explanation: Adverse selection occurs before a deal, when the better-informed party is more likely to take it up, as with high-risk buyers of insurance or sellers of faulty used cars. Moral hazard is a change in behaviour after the deal.

questions.stem: After insuring their car comprehensively, a driver starts parking it on the street rather than in a locked garage. This is an example of:
options: adverse selection, as risky drivers buy more insurance cover
a negative externality of production
a price ceiling in the insurance market
moral hazard, as insurance reduces the incentive to avoid risk
questions.explanation: Moral hazard arises when one party changes behaviour after an agreement because others bear the cost. Insurers respond with excesses and conditions that keep some of the risk with the insured.

questions.stem: A Pigouvian tax on a good that creates pollution is designed to:
options: raise as much revenue as possible regardless of its effect on output
lower the price consumers pay so that they buy more of the good
ban production of the good to eliminate pollution completely
make producers pay the external cost so output falls towards the social optimum
questions.explanation: Setting a tax equal to the external cost per unit internalises the externality, shifting supply up to MSC so the market produces the socially optimal quantity. The aim is efficiency, not zero output.

questions.stem: A government places a per-unit Pigouvian tax on a polluting good that is larger than the external cost per unit. The likely result is:
options: output rises above the free market level
the externality is fully corrected with no remaining loss to society as a whole
output falls below the socially optimal level, causing a new welfare loss
output falls to exactly the socially optimal level
questions.explanation: If the tax exceeds the marginal external cost, too little of the good is produced, which is a government failure. Valuing the external cost accurately is a key difficulty for this tool.

questions.stem: A government sets a minimum price for a farm product above its equilibrium price. The most likely result is:
options: a surplus, as quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
a shortage, as quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
no effect, as the market will return to its old equilibrium
a fall in farmers' incomes as their prices are reduced
questions.explanation: A price floor above equilibrium encourages more supply but discourages purchases, leaving unsold output. The government may then have to buy and store the surplus.

questions.stem: A price ceiling set below the equilibrium price of a good is most likely to cause:
options: a shortage, with queues, rationing or black markets
a surplus, with unsold stock building up in warehouses
a rise in the quantity supplied of the good
the market price rising above the ceiling legally
questions.explanation: At a price below equilibrium, buyers want more than sellers will supply, so the good must be rationed by other means. Price ceilings are intended to protect buyers but can reduce supply.

questions.stem: A government subsidises a merit good such as preschool education. If the subsidy is well designed, it should:
options: lower the price and raise consumption towards the socially optimal level
raise the price so that only the families who value preschool most will attend
reduce consumption to cut the welfare loss from over-consumption
remove the external benefits so the market becomes efficient
questions.explanation: Merit goods are under-consumed because buyers ignore some benefits to themselves or society. A subsidy lowers the price, increasing consumption towards the level where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost.

questions.stem: Suasion as a method of market modification means:
options: selling permits that allow firms to emit a set amount of pollution each year
having the government produce goods directly for the public
persuading people to change their behaviour through campaigns and information
taxing goods that create external costs to discourage their use
questions.explanation: Suasion, or moral suasion, relies on persuasion, such as anti-smoking or water-saving campaigns, rather than price changes or legal requirements. It is cheap but often slow and weak in effect.

questions.stem: Under a tradable permit scheme for pollution, a firm that can cut its emissions cheaply is likely to:
options: keep all of its permits and make no change at all to its level of emissions
pay a fixed tax on each tonne regardless of permits held
cut emissions and sell its spare permits to firms facing higher costs
buy extra permits so that it can increase its emissions
questions.explanation: Trading means emissions are cut by the firms that can do so most cheaply, so the total cap is met at the lowest overall cost. A fixed charge per tonne describes a tax, not a permit scheme.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of direct state provision as a method of market modification?
options: The government lets firms buy and sell pollution permits
The government operates public hospitals that treat patients without charge
The government sets legal rules on the exhaust emissions allowed from all new cars
The government runs advertising urging people to recycle more
questions.explanation: Direct provision means the government supplies the good itself, often because the market under-provides it. Emissions standards are regulation, advertising is suasion, and permits are a market-based tool.

questions.stem: A government bans the sale of single-use plastic bags. A possible unintended consequence is that:
options: shoppers stop buying groceries because they cannot carry them
shoppers buy thicker bags or bin liners, so plastic use falls less than expected
plastic litter falls by exactly the number of single-use bags previously sold
the market for plastic bags becomes perfectly competitive
questions.explanation: Unintended consequences arise when people respond to an intervention in ways policymakers did not expect. Evaluating a measure means considering such effects as well as the intended ones.

questions.stem: Which intervention is matched correctly with the market failure it addresses?
options: A subsidy for solar panels: adverse selection in insurance
A tax on cigarettes: under-provision of a public good
Mandatory product disclosure statements: asymmetric information
A price ceiling on rents: a negative externality of production in housing
questions.explanation: Disclosure rules give buyers information sellers would otherwise keep, reducing asymmetric information. A cigarette tax addresses a demerit good with negative externalities, not a public good.
